title: Minkowski Theory and Number Field Class Groups

items.title: Unscaled Minkowski embedding
items.statement: For a degree-n number field K of signature (r₁,r₂), σ:K→R^{r₁}×C^{r₂}≅R^n lists the real embeddings and one representative from each complex-conjugate pair, using real and imaginary coordinates. Its complex block has Euclidean norm (Σ_j |τ_j(x)|²)^{1/2}; no √2 scaling is applied.
items.strategy: Because n=r₁+2r₂>0, at least one listed embedding exists, so a zero image forces x=0. Real-linear independence of the images of a Q-basis follows from the nonzero all-embedding determinant theorem; replacing each complex-conjugate row pair by real and imaginary rows changes absolute determinant by a factor 2.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory v3.08
William A. Stein, Algebraic Number Theory: A Computational Approach

items.title: Full Euclidean lattice and covolume
items.statement: A full lattice Λ⊂R^n is the integer span of a real basis b₁,…,bₙ; its covolume is |det(b₁,…,bₙ)|.
items.strategy: If c is another integer basis, both change matrices have integer entries and are inverses, so their determinants are ±1. Hence the absolute determinant is basis independent, positive, and equals the volume of its half-open parallelotope once the volume theorem is invoked.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory v3.08
Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory

items.title: Fundamental parallelotope and finite bounded intersections
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a full lattice Λ=ΣZbᵢ, the half-open P={Σtᵢbᵢ:0≤tᵢ<1} tiles R^n uniquely by Λ-translates, has Lebesgue volume covol(Λ), and every bounded subset of R^n meets Λ in finitely many points.
items.strategy: Apply the inverse basis matrix to x, split each real coordinate uniquely into integer and fractional parts, and return the fractional point to P. The invertible linear change-of-variables theorem gives vol(P)=|det(bᵢ)| because [0,1)^n has unit volume. The inverse basis map sends any bounded set to bounded coordinate ranges, so only finitely many integer tuples occur.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory v3.08
Brian Conrad and Aaron Landesman, Math 154 Algebraic Number Theory

items.title: Blichfeldt lattice-point principle
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If S⊂R^n is Lebesgue measurable with vol(S)>covol(Λ), two distinct points x,y∈S satisfy x−y∈Λ.
items.strategy: Partition S among the disjoint half-open translates P+λ. Translate each measurable piece into P; their measures sum to vol(S), including when S is unbounded since Λ is countable via its integer coordinates. If every translated pair were disjoint, countable additivity would give union measure vol(S)>vol(P), impossible. An overlap supplies distinct points from different tiles with lattice difference; equality on tile boundaries is fixed by the half-open convention.

items.title: Minkowski convex-body theorem, strict form
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If measurable C⊂R^n is convex, centrally symmetric, and vol(C)>2^n covol(Λ), then C contains a nonzero point of Λ.
items.strategy: Dilate C by 1/2; its volume exceeds covol(Λ). Blichfeldt gives distinct u,v in C/2 with u−v∈Λ. Since 2u,−2v∈C, their midpoint u−v lies in C by convexity, and is nonzero.

items.title: Minkowski convex-body theorem at equality
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If C⊂R^n is compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and vol(C)≥2^n covol(Λ), then C contains a nonzero lattice point.
items.strategy: For m≥1 apply the strict form to (1+1/m)C. All resulting nonzero lattice points lie in 2C, whose lattice intersection is finite. One point occurs along an unbounded subsequence; its rescaled preimages converge to it in closed C. Compactness and the half-open tile argument handle the boundary case.

items.title: Successive minima of a convex body
items.statement: For compact centrally symmetric convex C⊂R^n with nonempty interior and a full lattice Λ, λᵢ(C,Λ) is the infimum of t>0 such that span_R(tC∩Λ) has dimension at least i, for 1≤i≤n.
items.strategy: The body contains a Euclidean ball about zero and is bounded, giving finite thresholds. For positivity, write the full lattice as B Z^n; boundedness of B^{-1} gives |Bm|≥1/K for every nonzero integer vector m, so a nonzero lattice point in tC forces t≥1/(KR). Nesting of dilates and a spanning dilate give 0<λ₁≤⋯≤λₙ<∞; the later attainment lemma proves the infima occur.

references.title: Ben Green, Additive Combinatorics, Lecture 3 §3.7
Martin Henk, Successive Minima and Lattice Points

items.title: Attained successive minima and adapted flag
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Each successive minimum λᵢ is attained. There are independent a₁,…,aₙ∈Λ with aᵢ∈λᵢC and span(λᵢC∩Λ)=span{aⱼ:λⱼ≤λᵢ}; moreover span(int(λᵢC)∩Λ)⊆span{aⱼ:λⱼ<λᵢ} for every i.
items.strategy: Approximate each infimum by a countable sequence of thresholds, then pass to a recurring subset of the finite lattice set in a fixed bounded dilate. Build the adapted basis by least indices from that finite set. For the interior flag, shrink an interior lattice point using continuity; when p=0 choose only this shrink parameter, and when p>0 also choose it below the finite positive gaps to the smaller minima, giving the dimension contradiction.

items.title: Triangular Borel maps scale Euclidean volume
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let aᵢ>0 and Borel ψᵢ:R^{n−i}→R. The triangular Borel bijection Tᵢ(x)=aᵢxᵢ+ψᵢ(x_{i+1},…,xₙ) sends Borel sets E to Borel sets and vol(T(E))=(∏aᵢ)vol(E); its inverse scales by (∏aᵢ)^{-1}.
items.strategy: Solve coordinates backward, so T and T^{-1} are Borel. Factor T into coordinate scalings and shears. For a shear, each one-dimensional fibre is translated by a Borel function of later coordinates, so translation invariance and Tonelli give equal measure. A positive coordinate scaling multiplies one-dimensional fibre length by aᵢ; Fubini/Tonelli and product–Euclidean identification give the formula for arbitrary Borel E, with extended values allowed.

references.title: Ben Green, Additive Combinatorics, Lecture 3 §3.7

items.title: Successive-minima volume deformation and collision avoidance
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For U=int(C), an adapted directional lattice basis aᵢ, and successive minima λᵢ, the slice-centroid triangular map Φ(U) is measurable, centrally symmetric, has volume (∏λᵢ)vol(C), and has no two distinct points differing by an element of 2Λ. In particular Φ(U)∩Λ={0}. Convexity of Φ(U) is not asserted.
items.strategy: Use the adapted vectors as a real coordinate basis. Each slice has positive finite relative volume and its centroid lies in the slice by separation in its affine hull. Paired slices satisfy F_j(-x)=-F_j(x), so reflection makes the centroid map odd without asserting that an individual slice is symmetric. Tonelli gives Borel coordinate ratios; the constant fibre Jacobian sqrt(det(AᵀA)) cancels. Exhaust int(C) by positive dilates with k≥2, apply triangular volume scaling, and use the adapted interior flag to exclude collisions modulo 2Λ.

items.title: Minkowski second theorem on successive minima
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a compact centrally symmetric convex body C⊂R^n with nonempty interior and full lattice Λ, (2^n/n!)covol(Λ)≤(∏_{i=1}^n λᵢ(C,Λ))vol(C)≤2^n covol(Λ).
items.strategy: Choose independent adapted aᵢ. The cross-polytope conv{±aᵢ/λᵢ} lies in C. Decompose the standard cross-polytope into 2^n orthant simplices, integrate each simplex to volume 1/n! by Tonelli, then apply the linear determinant formula; the resulting volume is 2^n|det(aᵢ)|/(n!∏λᵢ). because the aᵢ generate a finite-index sublattice, |det(aᵢ)|≥covol(Λ), yielding the lower bound. For the upper bound, the deformation lemma gives Borel Φ(int C) of volume (∏λᵢ)vol(C) and forbids 2Λ-congruent distinct points. If this volume exceeded covol(2Λ)=2^n covol(Λ), Blichfeldt would produce exactly such a pair. The boundary of a convex body has zero volume by nested homothetic approximation, so vol(int C)=vol(C).

items.title: Number-field integer rings and ideals are full lattices
items.statement: The unscaled Minkowski images of O_K and every nonzero fractional O_K-ideal are full lattices in R^{[K:Q]}.
items.strategy: A Z-basis of O_K is Q-independent after positive-denominator clearing and therefore a Q-basis; the published embedding-determinant theorem makes its realified images a real basis. Prove locally by induction that each subgroup of Z^n has a basis of at most n elements, projecting to dZ and adjoining one lift to a basis of the kernel. For a nonzero integral ideal a, uO_K⊂a makes its real span full, so its subgroup basis has exactly n members; Z-independence then gives Q-independence. For fractional I, dI is integral by definition, and invertible real block multiplication transports its lattice to σ(I). This proof uses no Choice.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory v3.08
William A. Stein, Algebraic Number Theory: A Computational Approach

items.title: Covolume of an integral ideal lattice
items.statement: With the unscaled embedding and a nonzero integral ideal a⊂O_K, covol(σ(a))=2^{-r₂}√|d_K|·Na.
items.strategy: For any Z-basis of a, form the all-complex embedding matrix B and the real matrix A obtained by replacing each conjugate pair by real and imaginary columns. Each pair changes |det| by factor 2, so |det A|=2^{-r₂}√|disc(a-basis)|. The integral inclusion a⊂O_K has index Na and change-of-basis determinant ±Na, giving |disc(a-basis)|=(Na)^2|d_K|. For a fractional ideal first multiply by a positive integer to become integral; never apply the displayed integral norm formula to a fractional ideal without that reduction.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory v3.08
William A. Stein, Algebraic Number Theory: A Computational Approach

items.title: Archimedean product region, volume and norm bound
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For t>0 put X_t={(x,z)∈R^{r₁}×C^{r₂}:Σ|xᵢ|+2Σ|zⱼ|≤t}, n=r₁+2r₂. Then X_t is compact, convex, symmetric, vol(X_t)=2^{r₁}(π/2)^{r₂}t^n/n!, and every point satisfies ∏|xᵢ|∏|zⱼ|²≤(t/n)^n.
items.strategy: Split real coordinates by signs and put each complex coordinate in polar form z=ρe^{iθ}. The angular integral is 2π, and u=2ρ contributes (π/2)u du; iterating the simplex integral over r₁ variables of weight 1 and r₂ variables of weight u gives t^n/n!, with every boundary negligible. Apply the n-variable AM–GM inequality to the r₁ entries |xᵢ| and the two copies of each |zⱼ|. The factor π/2 is tied to the unscaled real/imaginary convention.

items.title: Small nonzero element in a number-field ideal
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For nonzero integral a⊂O_K, some 0≠α∈a satisfies |N_{K/Q}(α)|≤(4/π)^{r₂}(n!/n^n)√|d_K|·Na.
items.strategy: Set t^n=n!(4/π)^{r₂}√|d_K|Na, so the product region X_t has volume exactly 2^n covol(σ(a)). Equality-form Minkowski yields nonzero σ(α)∈X_t∩σ(a). The embedding norm formula gives |Nα|=∏real|σᵢα|∏complex|τⱼα|²; the region lemma bounds this by (t/n)^n. Carry the unscaled covolume factor 2^{-r₂} through the volume equation.

items.title: Minkowski bound for ideal classes
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every class in Cl(O_K) contains an integral ideal b with Nb≤M_K=(4/π)^{r₂}(n!/n^n)√|d_K|.
items.strategy: The published number-field Dedekind corollary applies to O_K (with AC), so the CA-9 fractional-ideal group and invertibility theorems apply. For any class [I] choose a nonzero fractional representative I and 0≠u∈O_K such that b=uI^{-1}⊂O_K is integral, as the fractional-ideal definition permits. Small-element theorem gives 0≠β∈b with |Nβ|≤M_K Nb. Because (β)⊂b and b is invertible, a=(β)b^{-1} is integral; [a]=[b]^{-1}=[I], not [I]^{-1}. The identity ab=(β) and the integral ideal norm theorem give Na=|Nβ|/Nb≤M_K. If u changes, b changes by a principal factor, so the class assertion is independent of the preliminary denominator.

items.title: Finitely many ideals of bounded norm
items.statement: For every real B≥1, only finitely many nonzero integral O_K-ideals a satisfy Na≤B.
items.strategy: For a with Na=m, Lagrange applied to the finite additive group O_K/a gives mO_K⊂a. For each positive integer m≤B, ideals between mO_K and O_K correspond to ideals of the finite ring O_K/mO_K, hence form a finite set. A finite union over m≤⌊B⌋ completes the proof. This finiteness argument itself makes no Choice assumption.

items.title: Finiteness of the number-field class group
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The ideal class group Cl(O_K) is finite.
items.strategy: The finite set of integral ideals with norm ≤M_K surjects onto Cl(O_K) by the class-bound theorem. The class quotient is well defined by the published CA interface, so its image is finite. The Choice cost comes only through the class-bound and class-group route.

items.title: Class group generated by small prime ideals
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Cl(O_K) is generated by classes of nonzero prime ideals p with Np≤M_K.
items.strategy: Use the CA-9 proved unique factorisation theorem, under AC, to factor each bounded integral representative a=∏pᵢ^{eᵢ}. Multiplicativity of positive integer ideal norm gives each Npᵢ≤Na≤M_K, and the class of a is the product of their classes. The separately published ZF factorisation route is not substituted for this AC-qualified CA-9 supplier.

items.title: Nontrivial number fields have discriminant of absolute value greater than one
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If [K:Q]=n>1, then |d_K|>1.
items.strategy: At least one ideal class exists, so its bounded representative has norm ≥1, implying √|d_K|≥n^n/(n!(4/π)^{r₂}). Since r₂≤n/2, set U_n=(4/π)^{n/2}n!/n^n. At n=2, U₂=2/π<1; for n≥2, U_{n+1}/U_n=(2/√π)(n/(n+1))^n<1 because the binomial expansion gives (1+1/n)^n≥2+(n−1)/(2n)>2, hence (n/(n+1))^n<1/2. Thus U_n<1 and hence (4/π)^{r₂}n!/n^n<1. Therefore |d_K|>1; degree one is excluded explicitly.

items.title: Every nontrivial number field has a ramified finite prime
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every finite number-field extension K/Q with [K:Q]>1 has a rational prime that ramifies in K.
items.strategy: The preceding corollary gives an integer d_K with |d_K|>1, so some rational prime p divides it. The published ramification–discriminant criterion gives p ramified. Independently check that criterion here via the finite F_p-algebra O_K/pO_K: p divides d_K exactly when its trace pairing is degenerate; over the perfect field F_p this is equivalent to a nonreduced algebra, and the prime-power CRT decomposition is nonreduced exactly when some ramification index exceeds one. This concerns finite primes only.

items.title: Bounded roots give finitely many monic integer polynomials
items.statement: For fixed n≥1 and R≥1, there are finitely many monic integer polynomials of degree at most n whose complex roots, counted with multiplicity, all have modulus at most R.
items.strategy: For a monic degree-m polynomial f(X)=∏_{j=1}^m(X−α_j), Vieta gives each coefficient c_{m-k}=(-1)^k Σ_{|S|=k}∏_{j∈S}α_j, so |c_{m-k}|≤binom(m,k)R^k. For each m≤n, every coefficient lies in an explicitly finite integer interval; the finite union of boxes is finite. The constant polynomial 1 handles m=0 if included.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Number Theory v3.08

items.title: Bounded primitive integral element for Hermite–Minkowski
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For fixed integers n≥2 and real B≥1, every degree-n number field K with |d_K|≤B has α∈O_K with K=Q(α) and every conjugate of α of modulus at most √(B+2).
items.strategy: Use the real or totally complex convex window and compare its volume with the unscaled ideal-lattice covolume; the Gregory–Leibniz N=1 remainder proves π>2. The norm makes the distinguished real embedding exceptional in the real case and, for r₂≥2, makes the first complex pair uniquely larger than one. When r₂=1, the window point is a nonzero integral element with |Re τ₁(α)|<1, so it cannot be rational; degree two then makes it primitive. The windows give the common conjugate bound √(B+2).

items.title: Hermite–Minkowski finiteness
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For fixed positive integers n and B, only finitely many Q-isomorphism classes of degree-n number fields have |d_K|≤B.
items.strategy: For n=1 only Q occurs. For n≥2 the primitive-element lemma produces integral α generating each field and with every conjugate bounded by √(B+2); its monic degree-n minimal polynomial has integer coefficients. The bounded-polynomial lemma leaves finitely many such polynomials. Each irreducible polynomial determines at most one Q-isomorphism class Q[X]/(f), so the field set is finite. No generated field is counted merely from a nonprimitive integer.

title: Minkowski Theory and Number Field Class Groups — Examples

items.title: Minkowski bound for Gaussian integers
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For K=Q(i), M_K=4/π<2, so Cl(Z[i]) is trivial and Z[i] is a PID.
items.strategy: Use O_K=Z[i], d_K=−4, n=2 and r₂=1. The formula gives M_K=(4/π)(2!/2²)·2=4/π. Every bounded integral representative has positive integer norm 1, hence is O_K; the class group is trivial. Apply the published Dedekind PID criterion. The inequality uses π>2.

items.title: Class group of Q(√−5)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For K=Q(√−5), Cl(O_K)≅Z/2Z, generated by the class of p=(2,1+√−5).
items.strategy: O_K=Z[√−5], d_K=−20, so M_K=(2/π)√20<3 and integral class representatives have norm 1 or 2. A norm-2 quotient is F₂ and sends √−5 to its unique root 1, hence p is the unique norm-2 ideal. It satisfies p²=(2) by containment and equal norm 4, or the ramified prime factorization. If p=(a+b√−5), its norm would be a²+5b²=2, impossible. Thus p is nonprincipal of order two, and {1,[p]} exhausts the bound.

items.title: Class group of Q(√10)
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For K=Q(√10), Cl(O_K)≅Z/2Z.
items.strategy: O_K=Z[√10], d_K=40, n=2, r₂=0 and M_K=√10<4, so only norms 1,2,3 occur. The quotient maps give p₂=(2,√10) of norm2 and p₃=(3,1+√10), p₃′=(3,1−√10) of norm3, with no other ideals of those norms; show this by homomorphisms to F₂ and F₃. Explicit ideal containment and norm give p₂²=(2), p₃p₃′=(3), and p₂p₃=(4+√10) because N(4+√10)=6 and 4+√10 lies in both primes. Thus [p₃]=[p₂] and [p₃′]=[p₂]^{-1}=[p₂]. If p₂ were principal, a²−10b²=±2, impossible modulo 5; hence [p₂] has order exactly two, and the bound exhausts all classes.

items.title: Higher-degree class group by norm exclusions
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let α be a root of f=X⁵−X−1 and K=Q(α). Then O_K=Z[α], d_K=2869=19·151, M_K<4, and Cl(O_K) is trivial because no ideal has norm 2 or 3.
items.strategy: Over F₃, f has no roots and no irreducible quadratic factor, so it is irreducible over Q. Compute disc(f)=2869 via the resultant; its two distinct prime factors give the maximal power basis. The derivative has critical points ±c with f(−c)=4c/5−1<0 and f(c)=−4c/5−1<0, giving signature (1,2). The finite-remainder Gregory–Leibniz bound gives π>3 and hence M_K<4. Norm-two and norm-three ideals would yield roots of f modulo those primes, so every bounded class representative has norm one.

items.title: Signature constant rules out discriminant ±1
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every signature (r₁,r₂) with n=r₁+2r₂>1, the inequality 1≤(4/π)^{r₂}(n!/n^n)√|d_K| forces |d_K|>1.
items.strategy: Write the numerical constant C_{n,r₂}; check n=2 separately: C_{2,0}=1/2 and C_{2,1}=2/π. For n≥3 use r₂≤n/2 and the decreasing bound U_n from the preceding corollary, so C_{n,r₂}<1. Apply the class bound to any class and the fact its representative norm is a positive integer. This records exactly where the signature factor enters.

items.title: No nontrivial everywhere unramified number field over Q
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A finite number field K≠Q cannot be unramified at every finite rational prime.
items.strategy: If all finite primes were unramified, the discriminant criterion would make d_K a nonzero integer with no prime divisors, hence ±1. The discriminant lower-bound corollary rules this out for degree>1. State explicitly that the conclusion concerns finite primes, without silently adding an archimedean convention.

items.title: Mixing scaled and unscaled Minkowski covolumes fails
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For K=Q(i), the unscaled lattice σ(O_K)=Z² has covolume 1, while the √2-scaled lattice √2Z² has covolume 2. Using the unscaled value 1 as the latter covolume falsely predicts a nonzero lattice point in the disk of radius 6/5: its area 36π/25>4, but the shortest nonzero scaled-lattice vector has length √2>6/5.
items.strategy: Compute d_K=−4 and 2^{-r₂}√|d_K|=1 for the unscaled embedding. Scaling both real coordinates by √2 multiplies determinant by 2. Gregory–Leibniz partial sums N=7 and N=2 with opposite-signed remainders prove 3<π<4, placing the disk area 36π/25 strictly between the false threshold 4 and the true threshold 8; its radius remains below the shortest nonzero scaled-lattice length √2.
